definition: A concurrency model in which several threads in one process read and write the same variables directly. It is fast because nothing is copied, but the programmer must coordinate access with locks or atomics.
example: Four threads incrementing one global counter is shared-memory concurrency.

definition: An update made of three steps: read the current value, compute a new one, and write it back. If two threads interleave those steps, one thread's write can overwrite the other's, losing an update. An atomic read-modify-write performs all three as one indivisible step.
example: `counter += 1` reads counter, adds 1, then writes the result back.

definition: A race-condition bug where two threads read the same old value, both write a new value based on it, and one write silently overwrites the other. The final result is missing one of the changes.
example: Two threads read 7, both write 8: the counter should be 9 but one increment has been lost.

definition: One possible order in which the individual steps of several concurrent threads or tasks are mixed together when they run. Concurrency bugs appear only in some interleavings, which is why they are timing-dependent.
example: With two threads doing read then write, one interleaving is: T1 reads, T2 reads, T1 writes, T2 writes.

definition: A piece of code that accesses shared data and must not be run by more than one thread at a time. A lock is taken on entry and released on exit to enforce that.
example: The three lines between `with lock:` and the end of its block form a critical section.

definition: The guarantee that at most one thread is inside a given critical section at any moment. It is what a mutex (lock) provides.
example: Because both functions take the same lock, a sale and a refund are mutually exclusive.

definition: A synchronisation object that only one thread can hold at a time: a thread acquires it before touching shared data and releases it afterwards, and any other thread trying to acquire it waits. A mutex is the common kind; locks also make the holder's writes visible to the next thread that takes the same lock.
example: With `with lock: counter += 1` in Python, four threads each adding 1,000 always leave 4,000.

definition: Library types whose reads, writes and read-modify-write operations are atomic and properly ordered between threads. Java has `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicBoolean` and `AtomicLong`; C++ has `std::atomic<T>`; Rust has `AtomicUsize`, `AtomicI32` and others; Go has the `sync/atomic` package.
example: Two threads calling `fetch_add(1, ...)` on one `AtomicI32` always add 2 in total.

definition: Whether, and when, a write made by one thread can be seen by another. Without synchronisation, compilers may keep a value in a register and CPUs may delay or reorder writes, so another thread can keep seeing the old value. Locks, volatile fields and atomics provide the ordering that makes writes visible.
example: A plain boolean `stop` flag set by one thread may never be seen by a thread spinning on it.

definition: A Java field modifier: reads and writes of a volatile field are synchronisation actions, so a write happens-before every later read that sees it, and the compiler cannot cache the field in a register. It gives visibility and ordering, not atomic compound updates. C and C++ `volatile` means something different and does not provide thread synchronisation.
example: `volatile boolean stop` lets one thread reliably stop another's `while (!stop)` loop.

definition: A compiler optimisation that moves a computation that gives the same answer on every iteration out of a loop, so it runs once. It is legal for a plain field the loop never writes, which is why an unsynchronised stop flag may never be re-read.
example: `while (!stop) {}` can be hoisted into `if (!stop) while (true) {}`.

definition: The hardware protocol that keeps each CPU core's private cache consistent with the others when they hold copies of the same memory. It has a cost: cores writing the same data keep invalidating each other's copies, which slows shared-memory programs.
example: Two cores incrementing one counter bounce its cache line back and forth on every write.

definition: The part of a language specification that says which values a read may return when threads share memory, and therefore which compiler and CPU reorderings a program can observe. It is defined mainly through the happens-before relation.
example: Java's memory model is chapter 17.4 of the Java Language Specification.

definition: The ordering relation a memory model uses to say when one action's effects must be visible to another. If a write happens-before a read and no other write intervenes, the read sees that write. Program order within a thread, lock release then acquire, and volatile or channel communication all create happens-before edges; the relation is transitive.
example: Unlocking a mutex happens-before the next lock of that same mutex, so the next holder sees all the earlier writes.

definition: The order in which one thread's actions appear in its own source code. Within a single thread, an earlier action in program order happens-before a later one.
example: In `data = 42; ready = true;`, the write to data comes first in program order.

definition: Paired memory-ordering rules: a release operation (such as unlocking, or a release store) publishes all the thread's earlier writes, and an acquire operation (such as locking, or an acquire load) that observes it is guaranteed to see them. Together they create a happens-before edge between two threads.
example: A C++ `store(true, memory_order_release)` seen by a `load(memory_order_acquire)` makes the data written before the store visible.

definition: A memory-model relation between a release-type action in one thread and the acquire-type action in another that observes it, such as a volatile write and a later read that sees the value. It is one of the building blocks of happens-before.
example: In Java, an unlock of a monitor synchronises-with every subsequent lock of that monitor.

definition: The simple model of concurrency in which every execution behaves as if all threads' operations were interleaved into one global order, with each thread's operations kept in program order. Real hardware and compilers do not provide it by default; languages promise it only under conditions.
example: Under SC, if two threads each set their own flag then read the other's, at least one must see the other's flag set.

definition: Data-race-free implies sequentially consistent: a language guarantee that programs with no data races behave as if they were sequentially consistent. Java and Go give it; C++ gives it only to race-free programs that avoid weaker atomic orderings.
example: A Go program whose shared variables are all protected by mutexes can be reasoned about as a simple interleaving.

definition: Atomic operations with the weakest memory ordering: each operation is still indivisible and free of data races, but it does not order other memory accesses around it. They are fine for a simple counter but can produce outcomes no sequentially consistent interleaving allows.
example: Two threads can each store to one relaxed atomic and load the other, and both loads can see the old values.

definition: The part of a compiler that rewrites code to run faster or smaller while keeping the behaviour the language guarantees. It assumes the program obeys the language's rules, such as having no data races.
example: An optimiser may keep a loop variable in a register instead of re-reading memory.

definition: The official definition of the Java language, published by Oracle. Its chapter 17 defines threads, locks and the Java memory model.
example: JLS 17.7 permits a non-volatile long write to be split into two 32-bit halves.

definition: Reading a multi-part value while another thread is half-way through writing it, so the result mixes old and new parts and was never written by anyone. Java allows it for non-volatile `long` and `double`; Java uses "word tearing" for a separate problem, a write to one field clobbering an adjacent field, which it forbids.
example: A reader could see the new high 32 bits and the old low 32 bits of a 64-bit counter.

definition: Describes work whose speed is limited by computation rather than by waiting, such as parsing, hashing or number crunching. Only real parallelism on several cores speeds it up.
example: Computing a million SHA-256 hashes is CPU-bound.

definition: Describes work whose speed is limited by waiting for input/output, such as network replies or disk reads, rather than by computation. Concurrency helps because many waits can overlap.
example: A crawler fetching 1,000 web pages spends nearly all its time I/O-bound.

definition: Moving data between a program and the outside world: files, network sockets, terminals and devices. I/O is slow compared with computation, so programs spend much of their time waiting for it.
example: Reading a 1 MB file or a reply from a database server are both I/O.

definition: Python's standard module for running work in separate operating-system processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL, so CPU-bound Python code can use several cores. `ProcessPoolExecutor` is the higher-level process pool interface.
example: A four-process pool can run four CPU-heavy pure-Python jobs in parallel.

definition: A build of CPython without the GIL, added by PEP 703. It was experimental in Python 3.13 and is officially supported, though not the default, from 3.14. Threads can run Python bytecode in parallel on several cores.
example: Run `python3.13t` to try the free-threaded 3.13 build.

definition: The ability to combine two correct components and get a correct whole. Lock-based code composes badly: two modules that each lock correctly can deadlock when used together.
example: Module A locks X then Y, module B locks Y then X: each fine alone, deadlock together.

definition: A discipline for avoiding deadlock: every thread acquires multiple locks in the same agreed global order, so no waiting cycle can form.
example: If every thread always locks `a` before `b`, two threads cannot each hold one and wait for the other.

definition: A data-race detector built into the Clang and GCC compilers. It instruments memory accesses at compile time and reports conflicting accesses not ordered by happens-before while the program runs, at a cost of several times slower execution.
example: Compile with `-fsanitize=thread` to enable ThreadSanitizer.

definition: The Java Concurrency Stress tests harness from the OpenJDK project. It runs small concurrent snippets millions of times to find outcomes the Java memory model allows but you did not expect.
A tool that watches a running program and reports data races it actually observes. Go's is enabled with the `-race` flag; it can only find races on code paths that a test or run exercises.
example: `go test -race ./...` runs the tests with race detection on.

definition: A scheduler, usually on one thread, that repeatedly runs ready tasks until they wait, asks the operating system which waits have finished, and makes those tasks ready again. It lets one thread handle thousands of mostly-idle connections.
example: Node.js, Python's asyncio and browsers all run JavaScript or Python callbacks from an event loop.

definition: A unit of concurrent work managed by an async runtime: a coroutine that the event loop or executor has been told to run. In asyncio, wrapping a coroutine in a Task schedules it so it runs without being awaited first.
example: `asyncio.create_task(job())` turns the coroutine `job()` into a running asyncio task.

definition: A function that can suspend part-way through, keeping its local variables and position, and later resume from exactly that point. Generators, async functions, Lua coroutines and goroutines are all built on the idea. Melvin Conway described coroutines in a 1963 paper.
example: A Python generator suspends at each `yield` and resumes at the next `next()` call.

definition: In Python, a function defined with `async def`. Calling it does not run its body; it returns a coroutine object that runs only when awaited or wrapped in a task.
example: `fetch()` on an `async def fetch` returns `<coroutine object fetch>` and prints nothing.

definition: Scheduling in which a task keeps running until it voluntarily gives up control, for example at an `await` or `yield`. Switch points are predictable, but one task that never yields stalls all the others.
example: An asyncio task running a CPU loop with no `await` blocks every other task on the loop.

definition: Scheduling in which the scheduler can interrupt a running thread or task at almost any point and switch to another, without the task's cooperation. OS threads are pre-emptive; Go and Erlang pre-empt their lightweight threads too.
example: The kernel may pre-empt a thread in the middle of `counter += 1`.

definition: The queue of tasks that are able to run right now, waiting only for the scheduler to give them the thread. A task that is waiting for I/O or a timer is not on it.
example: After `await asyncio.sleep(0)` the task goes to the back of the ready queue.

definition: A scheduler's list of runnable threads or tasks. Go gives each processor slot (P) its own local run queue of goroutines, plus a global one.
example: An idle Go P steals half of a busy P's run queue.

definition: The Linux kernel interface for efficiently waiting on many file descriptors at once: a program registers sockets and asks which are ready, instead of checking each one.
example: An event loop on Linux calls `epoll_wait` to learn which of 10,000 sockets have data.

definition: The BSD and macOS kernel interface for waiting on many events (sockets, files, timers, signals) at once, playing the same role as Linux's epoll.
Windows' kernel mechanism for asynchronous I/O: the program starts operations and a completion port reports when each has finished.
The operating-system facility an event loop uses to wait for many sockets and timers at once and learn which became ready: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and BSD, IOCP on Windows.
Python's standard library for single-threaded concurrency with async/await: an event loop, tasks, timers, async networking and synchronisation primitives such as `asyncio.Lock`.
example: `asyncio.run(main())` starts an event loop and runs `main` to completion.

definition: In Python, any object that can be used with `await`: a coroutine, a Task or a Future. Awaiting one that is not ready suspends the current coroutine.
A place where a coroutine can pause and let other tasks run, such as an `await` or `yield`. In async/await code they are visible in the source; with green threads they are hidden inside calls.
example: Between two awaits, an asyncio task cannot be interrupted by another task on the same loop.

definition: When a piece of code is entered again before an earlier run of it has finished, for example by a callback or a nested call. It can break assumptions that code runs one invocation at a time. In actor frameworks, a reentrant actor may interleave requests at its await points.
An asyncio option (Python 3.12+) that starts running a new task's coroutine immediately, up to its first suspension, when the task is created, instead of on a later loop turn.
An asyncio function that runs several awaitables concurrently and returns their results in order. By default, if one raises, `gather` raises that exception but does not cancel the others.
example: `await asyncio.gather(f(1), f(2))` runs both and returns `[r1, r2]`.

definition: An asyncio function that wraps a coroutine in a Task and schedules it on the event loop, so it starts without being awaited. Keep a reference to the returned Task, or it can be garbage-collected.
An asyncio function that runs a blocking function on a separate worker thread and lets the caller await its result, so the event loop stays free.
example: `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url)` runs a blocking HTTP call off the loop.

definition: A mutex for asyncio tasks: `async with lock:` lets only one task at a time into a block, even across awaits inside it. It is not thread-safe.

A JavaScript object representing a value that will be available later: pending, then fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. `.then` callbacks and the code after an `await` run as microtasks once it settles.
example: `Promise.resolve().then(f)` queues `f` as a microtask.

definition: In JavaScript, a unit of work the event loop runs one at a time: the main script, a timer callback, an I/O callback or a UI event. Microtasks are drained between tasks.
example: A `setTimeout(f, 0)` callback is a task, so it runs after all pending microtasks.

definition: A JavaScript function that schedules a callback to run as a task after at least the given delay in milliseconds. A delay of 0 still waits for the current task and all microtasks to finish.
A JavaScript function that queues a callback directly on the microtask queue.
A Node.js function that queues a callback on a special queue that runs before promise microtasks, after the current operation finishes.
The specification's name for one independent JavaScript execution context with its own event loop, heap of objects and job queues. The main thread is one agent; each worker is another.

Separate JavaScript agents running on their own OS threads, created with Node.js's `worker_threads` module or the browser's Web Workers API. They communicate by messages and are the usual way to run CPU-heavy JavaScript in parallel.
A JavaScript runtime outside the browser, built on the V8 engine and a single-threaded event loop (libuv). Widely used for network servers.
In JavaScript, a value that counts as true in a condition. Every object, including any Promise, is truthy; only a few values such as `false`, `0`, `""`, `null` and `undefined` are falsy.
example: `if (isAllowed())` is always taken when `isAllowed` is async, because a Promise is truthy.

definition: A project that lets the ESLint code checker understand TypeScript. Its type-aware rules include `no-misused-promises`, which flags a Promise used where a boolean is expected, and `no-floating-promises`, which flags promises nobody awaits or handles.
Starting a piece of work without keeping a handle to it or waiting for its result. It is convenient, but errors are lost and nothing guarantees the work finishes.
example: `asyncio.create_task(send_email())` with the result discarded is fire-and-forget.

definition: Bob Nystrom's name (2015) for the split async/await causes: async ("red") functions can call ordinary ("blue") ones, but ordinary functions cannot simply call async ones and get a result, so async spreads up the call chain and libraries ship two versions.
example: Python's synchronous `requests` and async `httpx.AsyncClient` exist side by side because of function colouring.

definition: Using `await` directly in a JavaScript module's top-level code, outside any async function. It was standardised in ES2022.
A popular synchronous Python HTTP client. Its calls block the calling thread, so using it inside an asyncio coroutine stalls the event loop.
A Python HTTP client offering both a synchronous API and an async one (`httpx.AsyncClient`) that works with asyncio.
An asyncio-based HTTP client and server library for Python.
A Python web framework built on asyncio. It runs `async def` endpoints directly on the event loop and plain `def` endpoints in a thread pool.
The 99th-percentile response time: 99 % of requests are faster than it and 1 % are slower. It shows the slow tail that an average hides.
example: A p99 of 4 s means one request in a hundred takes 4 seconds or more.

definition: A fixed or bounded set of reusable worker threads that take tasks from a queue, avoiding the cost of creating a thread per task.
example: FastAPI runs plain `def` endpoints on a thread pool so they do not block the event loop.

definition: A widely used cryptographic hash function that turns any input into a 256-bit (32-byte) fingerprint. Computing it is pure CPU work.
A small integer a Unix-like operating system gives a process for each open file, socket or pipe. Each process has a limit on how many it may hold open.
example: Opening 20,000 sockets at once can hit the limit and fail with "Too many open files".

definition: An operating-system endpoint for network communication. A program reads and writes a socket much like a file; a read blocks, or in async code suspends, until data arrives.
A durable list of background work, often in a separate service, that worker processes take jobs from. Unlike an in-memory task it survives restarts and can retry failures.
Merging the results of several concurrent workers into one stream, for example all workers sending to one results channel.
Limiting how many operations run at once, for example with a semaphore of 100 or a fixed pool of workers, so a burst of work cannot exhaust connections, memory or the remote service.
example: With `asyncio.Semaphore(100)`, at most 100 of 20,000 fetches are in flight at once.

definition: An ordinary function or procedure: called, runs to the end (or throws), returns, and its stack frame is discarded. It has one entry point and cannot pause half-way and be resumed.
The part of an operating system or language runtime that decides which ready thread or task runs next and on which CPU.
example: Go's scheduler places goroutines on a small number of OS threads.

definition: A double-ended queue: a list that supports fast insertion and removal at both ends. Python's `collections.deque` is a common choice for a simple run queue.
example: `q.popleft()` takes the oldest task; `q.append(t)` puts one at the back.

definition: A scheduling policy that gives each ready task a turn in a fixed rotation, putting it at the back of the queue after its turn.
example: Tasks A and B alternate: A, B, A, B.

definition: A coroutine that saves only its own frame when it suspends, usually compiled into a state machine object of known size. A function it calls cannot suspend it, so every function on the path to a suspension point must itself be a coroutine: the cause of function colouring. Python, JavaScript, C#, Kotlin and Rust async functions and C++20 coroutines are stackless.
example: A Rust `async fn` compiles to a fixed-size future that can live inside a struct.

definition: A coroutine with its own separate call stack, so a function nested several calls deep can suspend the whole coroutine. Lua coroutines, Ruby Fibers, Python's greenlet and goroutines are stackful.
example: In Lua, a plain `helper()` call can run `coroutine.yield` and pause its caller's coroutine.

definition: In Rust, a value implementing the `Future` trait: a computation that may not have finished yet. An `async fn` returns one; it does nothing until an executor polls it, and its size is known at compile time.
example: `tokio::spawn(fut)` hands a future to the Tokio executor to drive to completion.

definition: Ruby's stackful coroutine type: a block of code with its own stack that can be paused with `Fiber.yield` and resumed later.
A Python library providing stackful coroutines (greenlets) implemented in C, which switch by saving and restoring parts of the C stack. gevent is built on it.

A Python library that provides green threads built from greenlets and an event loop (the hub). It monkey-patches the standard library so blocking calls switch greenlets instead of blocking the OS thread.
example: After `monkey.patch_all()`, ordinary `requests` calls in many greenlets run concurrently.

definition: A thread scheduled by a language runtime or virtual machine instead of the operating-system kernel. Green threads are cheap to create and switch, and the runtime parks them when they would block.
example: Goroutines, Erlang processes and Java virtual threads are green threads.

definition: A threading model in which each language-level thread is backed by its own OS thread. Simple and parallel, but each thread costs a kernel thread and a full stack.
example: Java platform threads and C++ `std::thread` are 1:1.

definition: A threading model in which many user threads (M of them) all run on a single OS thread. Switching is cheap, but it cannot use more than one core and one blocking system call stalls every thread.
example: gevent's greenlets on one hub thread are M:1.

definition: A threading model in which M user threads are spread over N OS threads, with M usually much larger than N. It combines cheap threads with multicore parallelism, at the cost of a sophisticated runtime scheduler.
example: Go might run 100,000 goroutines on 8 OS threads.

definition: A Unix operating system originally from Sun Microsystems, where early JVMs used green threads before switching to native threads.
The structure of Go's scheduler: G is a goroutine, M is an OS thread ("machine") and P is a processor slot holding a local run queue. An M must hold a P to run Gs, and there are GOMAXPROCS Ps.
example: With GOMAXPROCS=4, at most four Ms run Go code at once, each holding one P.

definition: A processor that the operating system can schedule a thread on: a physical core, or each hardware thread of a core with simultaneous multithreading.
example: A 4-core CPU with 2 hardware threads per core shows 8 logical CPUs.

definition: One independent processing unit inside a CPU chip. A 4-core CPU can run four threads truly in parallel.
A scheduling technique where an idle worker takes queued tasks from a busy worker's queue, keeping all cores busy without a central queue. Go's idle Ps steal half of another P's run queue.
The part of the Go runtime that adds waiting network sockets to the OS poller (epoll or kqueue) and parks the goroutines, so no OS thread blocks waiting for socket data.
To set a thread or task aside, not runnable, until something it waits for happens, freeing the underlying OS thread for other work.
example: When a goroutine reads an empty socket, the runtime parks it until data arrives.

definition: A Go runtime background thread that runs without a P and monitors the system: it retakes Ps from threads stuck in system calls, triggers pre-emption of long-running goroutines and polls the network.
A point in a running program where the runtime can safely stop a thread, for example for garbage collection, because it knows where all the pointers are.
example: Before Go 1.14, a call-free loop contained no safe point, so the GC could wait for it forever.

definition: Go 1.14's mechanism for stopping a goroutine that never reaches a cooperative check: the runtime sends the thread a signal (SIGURG on Unix) and the handler pauses the goroutine at the current instruction if it is safe.
A small asynchronous notification the kernel delivers to a process or thread, interrupting what it is doing to run a handler. Each signal has a name and number, such as SIGURG.
example: Go uses SIGURG to interrupt a spinning goroutine.

definition: Erlang's unit of concurrency: a green thread with its own small heap and mailbox, scheduled by the BEAM virtual machine. It shares no memory with other processes and communicates only by messages, making it an actor. It is not an operating-system process.
example: An Erlang node can run hundreds of thousands of processes.

definition: The BEAM's unit of work for scheduling, roughly one function call. Each process may use a fixed budget of reductions (4,000 in current OTP releases, 2,000 before OTP 20) before the scheduler switches to another process.
example: A tight Erlang loop is still pre-empted, because every iteration is a function call that costs a reduction.

definition: Code written in C or another native language and called directly from a managed runtime such as the BEAM or JVM. Because the runtime cannot pre-empt it, long-running native code can block a scheduler thread.
Separate BEAM scheduler threads reserved for long-running native code (NIFs) that cannot yield, so it does not block the normal schedulers that run Erlang processes.

A lightweight `java.lang.Thread` added in Java 21 (JEP 444) and scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. When it blocks on supported operations it unmounts, freeing the carrier, so ordinary blocking code can scale to very many threads.
example: `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` gives each submitted task its own virtual thread.

definition: A platform (OS) thread on which the JVM runs virtual threads. A virtual thread is mounted on a carrier while it runs and unmounted while it waits. By default there is roughly one carrier per CPU core, in a ForkJoinPool.

Attaching a virtual thread to a carrier thread to run it (mounting), and detaching it while it waits, saving its stack to the heap (unmounting). Unmounting is what lets a few carriers serve many blocked virtual threads.
example: `Thread.sleep(1000)` in a virtual thread unmounts it for the second.

definition: A representation of "the rest of the computation" from some point: what still has to run when a paused task resumes. Virtual threads store theirs on the heap; the code after an `await` is the awaiting function's continuation.
Java's standard API for talking to relational databases. Its calls block the calling thread while the database responds.
Java's basic abstract class for reading bytes from a file, socket or other source; its `read` methods block until data is available.

When a blocked virtual thread cannot unmount and so keeps its carrier thread occupied, making that carrier unavailable to other virtual threads. In JDK 21 to 23 blocking inside `synchronized` caused it; JDK 24 (JEP 491) fixed that case, but blocking in native code still pins.
example: Eight virtual threads pinned during slow JDBC calls can occupy all eight carriers.

definition: Java's built-in locking: a `synchronized` block or method acquires the monitor lock of an object on entry and releases it on exit, even if an exception is thrown. It provides both mutual exclusion and happens-before ordering.
example: `synchronized (this) { count++; }` makes the increment safe.

definition: The lock built into every Java object, taken by `synchronized`. Holding it gives a thread exclusive access to code synchronised on that object.
A Java lock class that the same thread can acquire several times. Unlike `synchronized` in JDK 21, blocking while holding it does not pin a virtual thread.
A Java thread pool designed for many small tasks, using work stealing. It is the default scheduler for virtual threads.
A snapshot listing every thread in a running program and the call stack each is in. It is the main tool for diagnosing stalls and deadlocks in JVM services.
Replacing functions or modules of a library at run time, without changing its source. gevent monkey-patches Python's `socket`, `time.sleep` and similar so they switch greenlets instead of blocking.
A Python module written in C (or another compiled language) and loaded by the interpreter. It runs native code that monkey-patching cannot intercept and the GIL does not cover once released.
The OpenJDK project that added virtual threads and structured concurrency to Java, including reworking `java.io` and `java.net` so their blocking calls cooperate with virtual threads.

Calling functions written in C from another language, through a foreign function interface. It is easy when the caller uses ordinary OS-thread stacks and awkward for green-thread runtimes, whose small movable stacks C code does not expect.

A component that runs submitted tasks for you, managing the threads or event loop underneath. Java's `ExecutorService` runs tasks on a thread pool; in Rust an async executor such as Tokio polls futures until they finish.
example: A Rust future does nothing until an executor polls it.

definition: The most widely used async runtime (executor plus I/O and timers) for Rust. `tokio::spawn` runs a future as a task, possibly on several worker threads, so it requires the future to be `Send` and `'static`.
An async executor and framework for embedded Rust that runs futures on microcontrollers without an operating system or heap allocation.
A small device, such as a microcontroller, that a program is compiled for, often with no operating system, little memory and no heap.
A call that does not return until its result is available, holding the calling thread the whole time, such as a synchronous socket read, file read or `time.sleep`.
example: `time.sleep(1)` inside an asyncio coroutine blocks the event loop for a second.

definition: Tony Hoare's 1978 model of concurrency: a program is built from sequential processes that share no memory and interact only by sending messages over channels. Go's goroutines and channels are its best-known descendant.
example: In CSP style, a worker receives a job on one channel and sends its result on another.

definition: In CSP, an independent piece of a program that runs its own steps one after another and shares no state with the others; it interacts only through channels.

A typed conduit that one concurrent process sends values into and another receives them from. In Go, `make(chan T)` creates one; sending and receiving can block, which makes a channel both a queue and a synchronisation point.
example: `ch <- "ping"` sends a string on a Go channel; `msg := <-ch` receives it.

definition: Which part of a program is responsible for a value: allowed to use or change it, and responsible for freeing it. Passing ownership through a channel means the sender stops touching the value. In Rust ownership is checked by the compiler; in Go it is a convention.
example: After sending a pointer to a buffer, a Go sender that respects ownership never writes to that buffer again.

definition: A Go channel with capacity 0, made with `make(chan T)`. A send waits until a receiver takes the value and a receive waits for a sender, so every transfer is a rendezvous.

A Go channel with a queue of fixed capacity, made with `make(chan T, n)`. Sends complete without a receiver while there is room; a send blocks only when the buffer is full and a receive only when it is empty.
example: With `make(chan int, 2)`, two sends succeed immediately and the third blocks.

definition: A meeting point where two concurrent processes must both arrive before either continues. A send on an unbuffered channel is a rendezvous between sender and receiver.
A block of memory that temporarily holds data passing between a producer and a consumer, smoothing out differences in their speed. Its capacity is how many items it can hold.
example: A channel with capacity 100 can absorb a burst of 100 sends.

definition: The two sides of a queue or channel: a producer creates items and puts them in; a consumer takes them out and processes them.
example: A web handler producing log events and a logger consuming them.

definition: The default value Go gives a variable of each type when nothing else is assigned: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, "" for strings and nil for pointers, maps and channels. A receive from a closed, empty channel returns it.
In Go, nil is the zero value of pointers, maps, slices and channels: "no object". Sending to or receiving from a nil channel blocks forever, which is used to switch off a case in a select statement.
example: Setting `a = nil` once channel `a` is closed stops `select` choosing it.

definition: A run-time failure that stops normal execution of the current goroutine or thread, unwinding its stack. In Go, a panic that no deferred function recovers crashes the whole program; in Rust a panic unwinds the panicking thread by default, or aborts the whole process if the program is built with panic = "abort".
example: Sending on a closed Go channel panics with "send on closed channel".

definition: Notifying every waiting party at once rather than one. Closing a Go channel is a broadcast: every goroutine blocked receiving on it becomes able to continue.
Go's standard way to carry cancellation and deadlines through a call tree. `ctx.Done()` returns a channel that is closed when the context is cancelled, waking every goroutine selecting on it.
Asking running work to stop early because its result is no longer needed. It is cooperative in most languages: the task is told, and must reach a point where it notices and cleans up.
example: When one child of an asyncio TaskGroup fails, the group cancels the others.

definition: Go's statement for waiting on several channel operations at once: it blocks until one case can proceed, choosing uniformly at random if several are ready. A `default` case makes it non-blocking.
example: `select` with a `time.After` case adds a timeout to a receive.

definition: Produced by a deterministic algorithm that gives results that look random and are evenly spread, rather than by a truly random physical process.
A Go channel type, written `<-chan T`, that can only be received from. The compiler stops code holding it from sending or closing.
A fixed number of workers that take jobs from a shared queue or channel and send back results, limiting how much runs at once.
example: Three goroutines reading a jobs channel form a worker pool.

definition: A Go counter for waiting on a group of goroutines: `Add` increases it, each goroutine calls `Done` when finished, and `Wait` blocks until it reaches zero.

A goroutine that never finishes, usually because it is blocked forever on a channel nobody will use again. It keeps its stack and everything it references, and the runtime does not report it unless every goroutine is stuck.
example: A sender stuck on an unbuffered channel after the receiver returned is leaked.

definition: A Go testing package from Uber that fails a test if goroutines are still running when it finishes, catching goroutine leaks.
A concurrent programming language from 1983, designed for the Inmos transputer, that implemented CSP almost directly.
A 1980s microprocessor from the British company Inmos, designed for parallel computing with built-in links for communicating with other transputers.
A concurrent language designed by Rob Pike in the late 1980s with first-class channels; an ancestor of Go's channels.
A concurrent language for the Plan 9 operating system, with channels and lightweight processes; an ancestor of Go.
A concurrent language for the Inferno operating system with typed channels; an ancestor of Go.
A Rust package or library, the unit the Rust compiler builds and the Cargo tool downloads.
example: `crossbeam` is a crate with concurrency tools.

definition: Rust's standard-library channel: many senders can send into it, but only one receiver takes values out.
A popular Rust crate of concurrency tools, including fast multi-producer, multi-consumer channels and scoped threads.
A queue with a maximum size: when it is full, producers must wait (or fail), which gives backpressure. An unbounded queue keeps growing, limited only by memory.
example: Python's `queue.Queue(maxsize=100)` blocks a producer once 100 items are waiting.

definition: An ordering rule in which items leave in the same order they arrived, like a queue at a shop.
A synchronisation primitive that lets threads sleep until another thread signals that some condition, protected by a mutex, may have changed.
example: A consumer waits on a condition variable until the producer signals that the job list is non-empty.

definition: A loop that keeps checking for something without ever blocking, using a whole CPU core while doing no useful work.
example: `while (!stop) { }` is a busy loop.

definition: A model of concurrency proposed by Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop and Richard Steiger in 1973. Everything is an actor: an entity with private state and a mailbox that handles one message at a time and, in response, can only send messages, create actors and decide how to handle its next message.
example: Erlang processes and Akka actors follow the actor model.

definition: The queue where messages sent to an actor wait until it handles them. In Erlang and by default in Akka it is unbounded, so a slow actor's mailbox can grow until memory runs out.
example: A logger receiving 50,000 events a second but writing 30,000 gains 20,000 mailbox messages every second.

definition: Erlang's approach of giving each process its own heap and collecting each heap separately, so one process's collection pauses only that process.
In Erlang, the identifier of a process, returned by `spawn`. Sending to it with `Pid ! Msg` delivers a message to that process's mailbox, whether it is local or on another node.

The guarantee, given by Erlang and Akka, that messages sent from one particular sender to one particular receiver arrive in the order they were sent. Messages from different senders have no order relative to each other.
example: If A sends m1 then m2 to B, B handles m1 first; a message C sent meanwhile may land anywhere.

definition: Large Erlang binaries (byte strings over 64 bytes) stored once in a shared area and passed between local processes by reference, with a count of users, instead of being copied.
Erlang's `receive` behaviour: it scans the mailbox from the oldest message and takes the first one matching any of its patterns, leaving the others in place for later.
example: With `[{log,a}, {reply,7}]` in the mailbox, `receive {reply, V}` takes `{reply,7}` and leaves `{log,a}`.

definition: A unique value created by `make_ref()`, used to tag a request so its reply can be recognised. The compiler optimises a receive that matches a fresh reference to skip messages that arrived before the reference was made.
Erlang's standard set of libraries and design principles for building reliable systems, including supervisors and behaviours such as gen_server.

Erlang's error-handling philosophy: write the normal case, let a process crash on anything unexpected, and rely on a supervisor to restart it in a known-good state, instead of trying to handle every error locally.
The normal, expected flow through a piece of code, in which nothing goes wrong.
A two-way connection between Erlang processes created with `link` or `spawn_link`: if one dies abnormally, an exit signal is sent to the other, killing it too unless it traps exits.
A one-way watch one Erlang process sets on another with `monitor`: when the watched process dies, the watcher gets a `{'DOWN', Ref, process, Pid, Reason}` message and is not killed.
The notice an Erlang process sends to its linked processes when it terminates, carrying the reason. An abnormal reason kills the receiver unless it traps exits.
Setting an Erlang process flag (`trap_exit`) so that exit signals from linked processes arrive as ordinary `{'EXIT', Pid, Reason}` messages instead of killing the process. Supervisors do this.
An OTP process whose only job is to start child processes, watch them and restart them according to a strategy when they fail. If restarts happen too often it gives up and fails itself.
A supervisor's rule for which children to restart when one dies: one_for_one, one_for_all or rest_for_one.
A supervisor restart strategy: when a child dies, restart only that child. Suited to independent workers.
A supervisor restart strategy: when any child dies, restart all the children. Suited to children that only make sense together.
A supervisor restart strategy: when a child dies, restart it and every child started after it. Suited to children that depend on earlier ones.
example: With children `[Db, Cache, Api]`, a `Cache` crash restarts `Cache` and `Api`.

definition: A per-child setting in an OTP supervisor: a permanent child is always restarted, a transient child only after an abnormal exit, and a temporary child never.

A supervisor's limit on restarts: if more than MaxR restarts happen within MaxT seconds, it terminates its children and exits, passing the failure up to its own supervisor. Erlang's default is 1 restart in 5 seconds; Elixir's is 3 in 5.
example: A child that crashes within 100 ms of every start trips Erlang's default on its second crash.

definition: A hierarchy of supervisors and workers: supervisors supervise workers and other supervisors, so a failure is retried locally first and escalates upward only if restarts do not fix it.

A failure caused by temporary conditions, such as a timeout or an unlucky race, that usually does not recur when the operation is retried. A deterministic bug, by contrast, fails the same way every time.
A set of open database or network connections kept ready and handed out to callers, avoiding the cost of opening a new connection per request.

A reusable OTP module that implements the generic part of a common process pattern (such as a server's receive loop), leaving the programmer to write callback functions for the specific part. gen_server and supervisor are behaviours.
The OTP behaviour for a client-server process. `gen_server:call` sends a request and waits for the reply (default timeout 5 seconds); `gen_server:cast` sends without waiting.
One running Erlang virtual machine with a name, which can connect to other nodes to form a cluster. Processes on different nodes message each other with the same `!` syntax as locally.

Being able to address something the same way whether it is local or on another machine. An Erlang pid works for a process on any node, although the network still makes remote messages slower and less reliable.

An actor toolkit for Scala and Java on the JVM. Akka Typed actors accept only messages of a declared type; a failing actor is stopped by default unless wrapped in `Behaviors.supervise`. Akka Streams adds flow control and Akka Persistence durable state. It moved to the Business Source Licence in 2022.
A delivery guarantee in which each message arrives once or not at all: never duplicated, but possibly lost, with no automatic retries. Akka's default.
A delivery guarantee in which each message is retried until acknowledged, so it is never lost but may arrive more than once; receivers must tolerate duplicates.
The effect of each message being processed once and only once. Networks cannot guarantee exactly-once delivery, so systems approximate it with retries plus deduplication or transactions.
Recognising and discarding repeated copies of the same message, usually by remembering each message's ID, so that retries do not cause the same effect twice.
Akka's request/reply pattern: send a message with a temporary reply-to address and get back a Future that completes with the reply or fails after a timeout.
Akka's fire-and-forget send: put a message in an actor's mailbox and continue immediately, with no reply expected.

An object standing for a result that will be available later, which can be waited on, polled or given callbacks. Java's `Future` and Scala's `Future` are examples; JavaScript calls the idea a Promise.
example: `executor.submit(task)` returns a Java Future; calling `get()` waits for the result.

definition: A source-available licence: anyone can read the code and use it for development and testing, but production use beyond what the licensor allows needs a paid licence, and each release converts to an open-source licence after a set period. Akka adopted it in 2022, with free production use for companies under US$25 million annual revenue and conversion to Apache 2.0 after 3 years.
An open-source fork of Akka under the Apache 2.0 licence, maintained by the Apache Software Foundation after Akka's licence change.
A .NET framework from Microsoft for building distributed applications from virtual actors called grains. It was used for the online services of the Halo games.

An actor that always exists logically and is addressed by an ID: the runtime creates (activates) it on some server when a message arrives and removes it from memory when idle. Introduced by Microsoft Orleans.
Orleans' name for a virtual actor: an object with an identity, state and behaviour that the runtime activates on demand and that processes one request at a time by default.
An Akka feature that spreads actors with IDs across the machines of a cluster and routes messages to them by ID, similar to Orleans' virtual actors.
The Distributed Application Runtime: an open-source set of building blocks for microservices, including a virtual-actor model.
A mailbox with a capacity limit: when full, new messages are rejected, dropped or make the sender wait. Akka offers them as an option; Erlang mailboxes are unbounded.
Mechanisms that stop a fast sender overwhelming a slow receiver, for example by having the receiver signal how much it can accept.
A network failure that splits machines into groups that cannot reach each other while each keeps running.
Ordering messages so that if sending one message caused another, every receiver sees them in cause-then-effect order. Erlang and Akka do not guarantee it across different senders.
An increasing counter attached to each message so the receiver can detect gaps, duplicates and reordering and put messages back in order.
A component that writes log records. In Erlang the standard `logger` application has overload protection that drops or samples events when it falls behind.
Deliberately dropping or sampling some work when a system is overloaded, so it keeps serving the rest instead of collapsing.

The rule that a concurrent task may not outlive the code block that started it: the block waits for all its children, and failures and cancellation propagate through it. Popularised by Nathaniel J. Smith's 2018 essay and his Trio library, building on Martin Sústrik's earlier work; Python's TaskGroup, Kotlin's coroutineScope and Java's StructuredTaskScope follow it.
example: An asyncio TaskGroup's `async with` block does not exit until every task created in it has finished.

definition: A Python async library by Nathaniel J. Smith built around structured concurrency, where tasks are started only inside nurseries.
Trio's structured-concurrency scope: tasks are started in a nursery block, and the block does not exit until they have all finished; if one fails, the others are cancelled.
A policy of stopping as soon as something goes wrong rather than carrying on. A fail-fast task scope cancels the remaining tasks when one fails.
The exception asyncio raises inside a task to cancel it, at its next await. Code may catch it to clean up but should re-raise it.

Python 3.11's structured-concurrency API: `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:` waits for every task created with `tg.create_task`, cancels the rest if one fails, and raises the failures as an ExceptionGroup.
A Python 3.11 exception that bundles several exceptions, for example from several failed tasks. `except* SomeError` handles the matching exceptions inside a group.
example: `except* KeyError` catches a KeyError raised by one task in a TaskGroup.

definition: A Kotlin function that creates a structured scope: it waits for all coroutines launched inside it and cancels them all if one fails.
A Kotlin structured scope in which one child's failure does not cancel its siblings.
A Kotlin scope not tied to any parent, so coroutines launched in it are unstructured; its use is discouraged.

Java's structured-concurrency API, designed for virtual threads: subtasks are forked inside a try-with-resources block, `join()` waits for them, and no subtask outlives the block. A preview API since JDK 21.
A Java feature that is fully specified but not yet final; it must be enabled explicitly and may change between releases.
The part of the Rust compiler that enforces the borrowing rules: references never outlive their data, and shared and mutable borrows never overlap.
A Rust trait with no methods that only records a property of a type for the compiler, such as Send, Sync or Copy.
A Rust trait, such as Send or Sync, that the compiler implements automatically for a struct when all its fields implement it.
example: Adding an `Rc` field to a struct silently makes the struct not Send.

definition: Rust's mutex marks itself poisoned if a thread panics while holding the lock; later `lock()` calls return an error to warn that the data may be half-updated.

Running cleanup code frame by frame back up the call stack after a panic or exception, destroying or dropping each frame's local values as it goes. A Rust panic unwinds the panicking thread by default; a C++ exception unwinds until a handler catches it.
Threads spawned inside `std::thread::scope` (stable since Rust 1.63). All are joined before the scope returns, so they may borrow local variables.
Rust's function for starting an OS thread. Its closure must be `Send + 'static`, because the thread might outlive the caller.
Waiting for a thread or task to finish. A thread's last action happens-before `join()` returns, so the joiner sees everything it wrote.
example: `t.join()` blocks until thread `t` has finished.

definition: A Tokio collection of spawned tasks that can be awaited together; dropping it requests that its tasks be aborted, without waiting for cleanup.
A Tokio function that runs blocking code on a separate thread pool so it does not stall the async worker threads.
The Rust project's name for its promise that safe Rust code cannot contain data races. It does not cover deadlocks or logic races.
Rust code inside `unsafe` blocks or implementations, where the programmer promises invariants the compiler cannot check. Safe Rust's guarantees hold only if that code is sound.

Identifiers rustc prints with each error: E0499 is "cannot borrow as mutable more than once at a time", E0277 is "trait bound not satisfied" (for example a type that is not Send), E0373 is a closure that may outlive a borrowed variable.

A race condition in which each step is synchronised but the sequence is not, such as checking a balance under one lock and writing under another. No data race is involved, so neither Rust nor race detectors catch it.
example: Two withdrawals both see 100 before either subtracts 80.

definition: Independent: one design choice can be combined with any choice of the other.
Waiting, often for growing random intervals, before retrying, so competing parties stop colliding.
A lock method that returns immediately with failure instead of waiting if the lock is held.
Java's thread-safe hash map: individual operations are safe from many threads, and `computeIfAbsent` performs check-and-insert atomically.
A value a read returns that no write ever produced. The Java memory model forbids them for most types.

A function marked `async` (`async def` in Python, `async function` in JavaScript, `async fn` in Rust). It may use `await` inside, and calling it gives back a coroutine, Promise or future rather than the finished result. Python's start lazily; JavaScript's run immediately up to the first `await`.
example: Calling an `async def fetch()` in Python returns a coroutine object without printing anything.

definition: To suspend and hand control back: a generator or coroutine yields a value to whoever resumed it, and more loosely a task yields when it gives the thread back to the scheduler so others can run, for example at an `await`.
example: `await asyncio.sleep(0)` yields to the event loop without actually waiting.

definition: A numbered version of the Go language and runtime; a new one ships about every six months. Go 1.14 (2020) added asynchronous pre-emption; Go 1.25 (2025) made GOMAXPROCS respect container CPU limits on Linux.

Rust notation requiring a type to be thread-safe. `T: Send` means type `T` must implement Send (movable to another thread); `T: Sync` means it must implement Sync (shareable by reference); `!Send` marks a type that is not Send; `'static` additionally forbids borrowed references to short-lived data.
example: `thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `Send + 'static`.

definition: A yearly edition of the ECMAScript (JavaScript) standard, named by year. ES2017 added async functions; ES2022 added top-level await.
A Clojure library that adds CSP-style channels and lightweight `go` blocks to the JVM and JavaScript.
A point in the browser's event loop, such as the end of each task or callback, where it runs every queued microtask, including ones queued while draining, before continuing.

A chain of stages where each stage's output is the next stage's input. In Go each stage is a goroutine connected to the next by a channel, so stages run concurrently and closing a channel ripples down the chain.
example: `gen` → `sq` → `main` turns 2, 3, 4 into 4, 9, 16.

definition: How long a concurrent task exists, from being started to finishing or being cancelled. Unstructured spawns can outlive the code that started them; structured concurrency ties each task's lifetime to a block. (In Rust, lifetimes are also the compiler-checked spans for which references are valid.)
example: An asyncio task created inside a TaskGroup cannot outlive the `async with` block.
